definitions.definition: The act of braking, of using a brake to slow down a machine or vehicle
(engineering) An apparatus for testing the power of a steam engine or other motor by weighing the amount of friction that the motor will overcome; a friction brake.
(figuratively) Something used to retard or stop some action, process etc.

A device used to slow or stop the motion of a wheel, or of a vehicle, usually by friction (although other resistive forces, such as electromagnetic fields or aerodynamic drag, can also be used); also, the controls or apparatus used to engage such a mechanism such as the pedal in a car. [from 18th c.]
(obsolete) The winch of a crossbow. [14th–19th c.]
(military) An ancient engine of war analogous to the crossbow and ballista.
(chiefly nautical) The handle of a pump.
A baker’s kneading trough.

quote.citation: 1617, Gervase Markham, Cavalarice the English Horseman:
quote.text: You shall kneade […] first with handes‥lastly with the brake.

definitions.definition: A frame for confining a refractory horse while the smith is shoeing him.
An enclosure to restrain cattle, horses, etc.

quote.citation: 1868, March 7, The Illustrated London News, number 1472, volume 52, “Law and Police”, page 223:
quote.text: He was shooting, and the field where the [cock-fighting] ring was verged on the shooting-brake where the rabbits were.

definitions.definition: A cart or carriage without a body, used in breaking in horses.W
A carriage for transporting shooting parties and their equipment.W

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: It had been arranged as part of the day’s programme that Mr. Cooke was to drive those who wished to go over the Rise in his new brake.

quote.citation: 1976, Terrance Dicks, chapter 1, in Doctor Who and the Loch Ness Monster, page 11:
quote.text: A few moments later they heard the sound of an engine, and a muddy shooting brake appeared on the road behind them.

definitions.definition: A device used to confine or prevent the motion of an animal.
That part of a carriage, as of a movable battery, or engine, which enables it to turn.
(intransitive) To operate a brake or brakes.
(intransitive) To be stopped or slowed (as if) by braking.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Apparently a shortened form of bracken. (Compare chick, chicken.)

definitions.definition: A fern; bracken (Pteridium). [from 14th c.]
Any fern in the genus Pteris.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old English *bracu, attested in a plural compound form fearnbraca (“thickets of fern”), probably from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”) and influenced by sense 2 (“fern”). Compare Middle Low German brake (“stump, branch”).

definitions.definition: A thicket, or an area overgrown with briers etc. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1593, [William Shakespeare], Venus and Adonis, London:  […]  Richard Field, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Rounds rising hillocks, brakes obscure and rough, / To shelter thee from tempest and from rain.

quote.citation: 1808 February 22, Walter Scott, “(please specify the introduction or canto number, or chapter name)”, in Marmion; a Tale of Flodden Field, Edinburgh:  […]  J[ames] Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Company, […]; London: William Miller, and John Murray, →OCLC:
quote.text: He stayed not for brake, and he stopped not for stone.
He halts, and searches with his eyesAmong the scatter’d rocks:And now at distance can discernA stirring in a brake of fern  […]

quote.citation: 1859, George Meredith, chapter 5, in The Ordeal of Richard Feverel. A History of Father and Son. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London: Chapman and Hall, →OCLC:
quote.text: The bird, with its fellow in the break, drummed, and whirred, and to the misfortune of its species made its plumage seem a prize to them.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Late Middle English, from Middle Low German brake, Dutch braak, Old Dutch braeke; possibly related to sense 1.

definitions.definition: (textiles) A tool used for breaking flax or hemp. [from 15th c.]
A type of machine for bending sheet metal. (See wikipedia.)
A large, heavy harrow for breaking clods after ploughing; a drag.
(transitive) To bruise and crush; to knead.
(transitive) To pulverise with a harrow.
(obsolete) A cage. [16th–17th c.]
(now historical) A type of torture instrument. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 2011, Thomas Penn, Winter King, Penguin, published 2012, page 83:
quote.text: Methods of applying pain were many and ingenious, in particular the ways of twisting, stretching and manipulating the body out of shape, normally falling under the catch-all term of the rack, or the brakes.

definitions.definition: (archaic) simple past of break

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 32:3:
quote.text: And all the people brake off the golden earrings  […]
